hook.line: Mariana has been interrupted three times in one meeting, and she is not finished telling you about it. Here is how she says it.
hook.es: Me da rabia que me interrumpan.
hook.en: It makes me mad that they interrupt me.

examples.es: Me da rabia que Altamira compre todo.
examples.en: It makes me mad that Altamira buys everything.

examples.es: Me da rabia perder el bus.
examples.en: Missing the bus makes me mad.

examples.es: A Mariana le da mucha rabia que la interrumpan.
examples.en: It makes Mariana really mad that they interrupt her.

examples.es: ¿Te da rabia que no te escuchen?
examples.en: Does it make you mad that they don't listen to you? (to a friend)

examples.es: Nos da rabia que nadie nos diga nada.
examples.en: It makes us mad that nobody tells us anything.

rule:
*Rabia* is a noun, so Spanish doesn't say "I am mad" here. It says the thing gives you anger: *me da rabia*.

Someone else's action: *que* plus the wish form. *Me da rabia que me interrumpan.*
Your own action: the infinitive. *Me da rabia perder el bus.*

It's stronger than *me molesta*. Add *mucha* or *muchísima* to turn it up, or just say *¡Qué rabia!* on its own.
smallPrint: Very common in Colombia. *Rabia* is anger at everyday strength, so it fits a missed bus as well as a real injustice.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *interrumpen* or *interrumpan* and type the whole sentence: *Me da rabia que me ___.*
yourTurn.answer: Me da rabia que me interrumpan.
yourTurn.why: After *me da rabia que*, the verb takes the wish form: *interrumpan*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Missing the bus makes me mad.
yourTurn.answer: Me da rabia perder el bus.
yourTurn.why: It's your own action, so no *que*: just the infinitive.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: It makes me mad that Altamira buys everything.
yourTurn.answer: Me da rabia que Altamira compre todo.
yourTurn.why: Altamira acts, so *que* plus the wish form: *compre*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about all of us: *Me da rabia que nadie me diga nada.*
yourTurn.answer: Nos da rabia que nadie nos diga nada.
yourTurn.why: For *we*, both little words change: *me* becomes *nos*, twice.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish, to a friend: Does it make you mad that they don't listen to you?
yourTurn.answer: ¿Te da rabia que no te escuchen?
yourTurn.why: *Te* is you, and *escuchen* is the wish form for *ellos*.

yourTurn.prompt: Turn it up: *Me da rabia perder el bus.* (it makes me really, really mad)
yourTurn.answer: Me da muchísima rabia perder el bus.
yourTurn.why: *Muchísima* goes before *rabia* and agrees with it.
The bare reaction needs nothing else.

pitfalls.wrong: Me da rabia que me interrumpen.
pitfalls.right: Me da rabia que me interrumpan.
pitfalls.why: Almost. After *me da rabia que*, the verb takes the wish form: *interrumpan*.

pitfalls.wrong: Me da rabia que perder el bus.
pitfalls.right: Me da rabia perder el bus.
pitfalls.why: Almost. When you're the one acting, drop *que* and use the infinitive.

pitfalls.wrong: Yo doy rabia que Altamira compre todo.
pitfalls.right: Me da rabia que Altamira compre todo.
pitfalls.why: In English you're the one who is mad. In Spanish the event gives you the anger, so you become *me*.

personal: Tell us something that makes you mad. For example: *Me da rabia esperar tanto.* or *Me da rabia que nadie me diga nada.*
